meaning: In this verse, to be destroyed or wiped out, as all living things were killed by the flood.

idiom: a wild donkey of a man
meaning: A person like the wild donkey of the desert: untamed, fiercely independent, roaming free and refusing any yoke. He would always be fighting his neighbors and they him, yet would hold his ground.
Live all of life knowing you are always in God's sight: obeying Him, trying to please Him, and relying on Him in everything.
In this verse, to be destroyed or wiped out, as all living things were killed by the flood.

idiom: possess the gates of their enemies
meaning: To defeat enemies and take control of their cities and land. A city's gate stood for the city itself, its defenses, and its seat of government, so holding the gate meant ruling the city.
You have made me hated by the people of the land, which leaves us exposed to their revenge.

idiom: I will go down to Sheol mourning for my son
meaning: You will cause my death in old age through grief; I would spend the rest of my life in sorrow until I go to the grave.
To be held guilty and punished for someone's death, as God demands payment for shed blood.

idiom: you will bring my gray hair down to Sheol in sorrow
meaning: You will cause my death in old age through grief; I would spend the rest of my life in sorrow until I go to the grave.

idiom: Joseph's own hands will close your eyes
meaning: Closing a dead person's eyes was the last loving duty of the closest relative. The promise meant Jacob would die in peace with Joseph alive and at his side.

idiom: you went up to your father's bed
meaning: Reuben had sex with his father Jacob's concubine Bilhah. This shameful sin against his father cost him the rights of the firstborn.

idiom: nor the staff from between his feet
meaning: The ruler's staff, held between the feet of a seated king or judge, stands for authority; the line means rule will stay with Judah, possibly also through Judah's descendants.

idiom: The scepter will not depart from Judah
meaning: The right to rule and lead will stay with the tribe of Judah and its descendants until the promised one comes, the one the nations will obey. Commentators differ on whether tribal or royal power is meant, and on what "Shiloh" means.

Issachar is likened to a sturdy, big-boned work donkey, strong and fit to carry loads. The tribe would be hardy farm laborers who valued rest in their pleasant land so much that they would accept heavy burdens and tribute rather than fight for their freedom.

idiom: Naphtali is a doe set free
meaning: Most read it as picturing the tribe as swift, agile, and free, like a gazelle running loose (often a warrior image), perhaps also enjoying a fertile land; others repoint the Hebrew to read "a spreading terebinth putting out fine branches."

The children were born while Joseph was alive and were received by him. Some take this as Joseph, the family head, formally adopting or acknowledging them as his own. Others say it only means he held them on his lap and loved them.
God's own power acting directly, with no human go-between; here it strikes Egypt's livestock with a deadly plague as a judgment.
The offender would be expelled from the community of Israel and lose its privileges, with God himself threatening to step in and root him out.

idiom: a hand was lifted up toward the throne of the LORD
meaning: Either a solemn oath, made with a hand raised toward God's throne in heaven, that war on Amalek would never end; or a charge that Amalek had raised its hand against God's throne by attacking God's people. Some scholars change the word to "banner" instead.

idiom: Do not draw near to a woman
meaning: Do not have sexual relations, even with your own wife, so as to stay ritually pure for a solemn holy event.

idiom: the LORD will break out against them
meaning: If they cross the boundary, God will suddenly strike them with deadly judgment.

idiom: He will break out against them
meaning: If they cross the boundary, God will suddenly strike them with deadly judgment.

idiom: visiting the iniquity of the fathers on their children
meaning: God lets the punishment and consequences of parents' sin, especially idolatry, fall on their descendants for several generations. Examples include disease, poverty, and bad example. This applies above all to children who keep on hating God and follow their fathers' ways.

idiom: take the name of the LORD your God in vain
meaning: To misuse God's name for something empty or false. Some sources say it mainly forbids swearing a false oath in God's name; others say it also covers careless, frivolous, or insincere use, such as casual oaths, cursing, or magic.
Living in your towns and settlements. "Gates" stands for the cities, so the phrase means the foreigner who has settled among the Israelites in their land.

idiom: eye for eye, tooth for tooth
meaning: The law that the penalty must match the injury, no more and no less. It was a rule for judges and courts, not a license for personal revenge, and was often settled by a matching payment rather than literal maiming.

idiom: I will fulfill the number of your days
meaning: To let people live out their full natural lifespan with no early death, as a sign of God's blessing.
The high priest, through his consecrated office, took on himself the guilt and flaws attached to the people's sacred offerings and removed them, so that God would accept the gifts.

idiom: cut off from among his people
meaning: A Sabbath-breaker put himself outside God's covenant and was treated as an outlaw, expelled from the people. Some take it as another way of saying execution, or as a death sent by God when the crime was secret.
Stubborn and rebellious. The picture is a work animal that stiffens its neck and refuses to be steered by its driver or to accept the yoke.

idiom: He will visit the iniquity of the fathers on their children
meaning: God lets the punishment and consequences of parents' sin, especially idolatry, fall on their descendants for several generations. Examples include disease, poverty, and bad example. This applies above all to children who keep on hating God and follow their fathers' ways.

To worship other gods or idols. Israel was seen as bound to God like a wife to a husband, so idolatry was treated as unfaithfulness in marriage. The phrase also fits the sexually impure rites that went with some pagan worship.

idiom: the salt of the covenant of your God
meaning: A lasting agreement that cannot be broken. Salt keeps things from spoiling, it went with sacrifices, and sharing salt at a meal sealed friendship and loyalty, so a salt covenant stood for something permanent and binding.

idiom: a man lies with a woman
meaning: To have sexual relations with a woman, not merely to lie on the same bed.
To have sexual relations with a woman, not merely to lie on the same bed.

idiom: cut him off from among his people
meaning: God himself would turn his anger on anyone who ate blood and remove that person from the community, usually by death, especially when the offense was hidden from human judges.

idiom: I will set My face against that person
meaning: God turns toward someone with a fixed, hostile resolve. It means he is determined to oppose them in anger and bring punishment on them.
He stays guilty and must face the penalty for his offense.

idiom: cut him off from his people
meaning: God would remove the offender from his people by death. Some take this to mean that the people's stoning of him is God's own way of cutting him off; others take it to mean that God himself would strike him down if the crime went unpunished for lack of evidence.
To look the other way on purpose: to wink at or tolerate the crime and not accuse or punish the offender, whether from indifference or from quiet approval.

To worship other gods or idols. Israel was seen as bound to God like a wife to a husband, so idolatry was treated as unfaithfulness in marriage. The phrase also fits the sexually impure rites that went with some pagan worship.

idiom: cut off from among their people
meaning: Both offenders would be removed from the community. Some see a formal public expulsion, while others take it as death by the authorities or by God, or as dying without children.
To be held responsible for a sin and so face its punishment.
To "afflict the soul": to fast and deny oneself ordinary comforts, together with inner sorrow and repentance for sin, as on the Day of Atonement.

idiom: fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth
meaning: The law that the penalty must match the injury, no more and no less. It was a rule for judges and courts, not a license for personal revenge, and was often settled by a matching payment rather than literal maiming.
Put away the inner stubbornness, corrupt desires, and dullness toward God. Make real in the heart the purity and devotion to God that outward circumcision stood for.
In this verse, a wife turning aside from her husband into sexual unfaithfulness.
In this verse, a wife turning aside from her husband into sexual unfaithfulness.
He stays guilty and must face the penalty for his offense.

idiom: cause His face to shine upon you
meaning: A request for God's favor and kindness, a prayer that He would look on the speaker with grace and show His presence; it echoes the priestly blessing of Numbers 6.

idiom: lift up His countenance toward you
meaning: For God to turn His face toward someone and look at them with special care and favor.

idiom: Is the LORD's arm too short?
meaning: God asks whether his reach and strength are too limited to do what he promised. It is a rebuke to doubt: his power has no limit, and his word will come true.

idiom: they will be like bread for us
meaning: The enemy would be as easy to consume as food, so Israel would swallow them up and defeat them easily; some add that the enemy's goods would end up feeding Israel.
All together at one time, in a single sudden blow, as one person might be struck down.

idiom: You have taken too much upon yourselves!
meaning: Literally "enough for you": you have gone too far and claimed more than your right; you have held power and the priesthood long enough and set yourselves above others.
Literally "enough for you": you have gone too far and claimed more than your right; you have held power and the priesthood long enough and set yourselves above others.

idiom: bear the iniquity involving the sanctuary
meaning: The priests and Levites were answerable for any offense against or defilement of the holy place, whether done by themselves or by the people. They would suffer the penalty for it, and through their office they would also deal with that guilt and remove it.

A lasting agreement that cannot be broken. Salt keeps things from spoiling, it went with sacrifices, and sharing salt at a meal sealed friendship and loyalty, so a salt covenant stood for something permanent and binding.

The Levites were held responsible for guarding the sanctuary. They would carry the guilt and penalty for failures or neglect in that duty, including any wrongful approach by the people that they allowed.

idiom: Aaron will be gathered to his people
meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: Water will flow from his buckets
meaning: Israel will have overflowing blessing and prosperity. The picture is a man whose two buckets are so full they spill over, and in that dry region plentiful water was the main source of prosperity.

idiom: A star will come forth from Jacob, and a scepter will arise from Israel
meaning: A glorious king will rise from Israel. A star stood for royal splendor and a scepter for ruling power. The ruler would defeat Israel's enemies. It was applied first to David and above all to the Messiah.

idiom: Why should the name of our father disappear from his clan
meaning: Why should our father's family line and his share of land die out just because he had no son? His name lived on through holding an inheritance passed to descendants.

idiom: go out and come in before them
meaning: A leader who heads the people in all their affairs, in war and in daily life; leading them out and bringing them in pictures a shepherd guiding his flock.

idiom: will go out and come in
meaning: Joshua and the people would go out to war and come back, or carry out any undertaking, only at the direction given through the priest's inquiry of God.
If a husband let his wife's vow stand at first and then later forced her to break it, the guilt and penalty for the broken vow fell on him instead of on her.
The cruel bondage and suffering Israel went through in Egypt, compared to the intense heat of a furnace used to smelt iron.
Any human being, mankind, stressing that humans are weak and mortal.
God punishes those who hate Him personally, openly, and without delay, so that they see and feel it themselves in their own lifetime. The punishment is not put off to later generations.
Stubborn and rebellious. The picture is a work animal that stiffens its neck and refuses to be steered by its driver or to accept the yoke.

idiom: The sky over your head will be bronze, and the earth beneath you iron
meaning: A curse of severe, long drought. The sky stays hard and gives no rain or dew, and the ground turns hard and barren so nothing grows. God refuses to take the drought away.

idiom: the watered land as well as the dry
meaning: A proverbial phrase that is read in very different ways. Several commentators take it to mean destruction that sweeps away everything together, wet and dry alike: the whole people, both those already taken in by idolatry and those still drawn to it. Others (following the older reading "add drunkenness to thirst") take it as piling sin on sin, or as one sinner corrupting others.
Moses can no longer carry out his active work as leader among the people.
The pupil of the eye, the most delicate and closely guarded part of the body; it stands for someone kept with the greatest care and tenderness, a deeply cherished object.
They became well fed and prosperous from the land's plenty, and the luxury made them proud, self-indulgent and forgetful of God (as in "grew fat and kicked").
To have such plenty, especially of olive oil from a fertile land, that it could be used freely even on the feet. It stands for rich prosperity.

idiom: rolled away the reproach of Egypt
meaning: God removed a disgrace that had clung to Israel since Egypt, marked by their circumcision and their arrival in the promised land. Sources disagree about what the disgrace was: Egyptian taunts that God had led them out only to die in the desert, the shame of having been slaves, or their uncircumcised state.

idiom: from the hand of the LORD
meaning: In this verse, being delivered out of the hand of the LORD means being spared the punishing judgment that would otherwise have fallen on the whole people.

idiom: going the way of all the earth
meaning: To be about to die, taking the road every human must take sooner or later.
To turn the heart toward the LORD fully and willingly, loving, fearing, and serving him alone. This means giving up any hidden attachment to other gods, including idols of the heart.
To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your possession
meaning: A mocking, cowardly question: "Have you already captured and beaten these kings?" Until victory was certain, they would not risk the kings' revenge by helping Gideon.

idiom: If you had not plowed with my heifer
meaning: Using another man's heifer to plow meant getting results through someone else. Samson is saying they did not solve the riddle by their own wits but by working on his wife to get the secret. The sources reject the view that it hints at adultery.
The whole land of Israel, from its northern edge (Dan) to its southern edge (Beersheba). In other words, all Israel.

idiom: the ears of all who hear it will tingle
meaning: The news will be so shocking and terrible that anyone who hears it will be stunned, as if both ears had been struck.

idiom: His hand is heavy upon us
meaning: God's afflicting hand presses hard on the sufferer, so his pain is greater than even his groaning shows. Some read the Hebrew in Job 23:2 as Job's own hand weighing on or holding back his groans, and the verse's wording is unclear.

idiom: Israel has become a stench to the Philistines
meaning: Israel had become hated by the Philistines, who were provoked and angered against them.

idiom: a man after His own heart
meaning: A man God chose who fits what God wants, someone who would carry out God's will (David, in contrast to Saul).
He was refreshed and got his strength back. The dimness and faintness of hunger and exhaustion left him, and this showed in his eyes becoming clear and lively again.
David's family and descendants, which is why Jonathan's covenant reached past David himself to his line after him.

idiom: march in and out with me
meaning: David's conduct and service with Achish in the army, which Achish found trustworthy.

idiom: Your blood be on your own head
meaning: The guilt and responsibility for a person's death rests on that person (or on whoever is named), not on anyone else. Someone who dies through his own neglect or choice has only himself to blame.

idiom: the bow of Jonathan did not retreat
meaning: Jonathan's arrows never missed; they always struck and killed the enemy. The poetic picture is of weapons that "drink" the blood of the slain, praising him as a deadly, victorious warrior.

idiom: the house of Saul and the house of David
meaning: David's family and descendants, which is why Jonathan's covenant reached past David himself to his line after him.

idiom: Am I the head of a dog
meaning: An angry denial: "Am I something utterly worthless and contemptible, and a traitor siding with Judah?" Dogs were despised scavengers, so "dog" was an insult.

idiom: May it whirl over the head of Joab
meaning: A forceful curse: may the guilt and punishment for Abner's blood come crashing down on Joab and his family, so that his line always suffers disease, weakness, violent death, or poverty.

idiom: led Israel out and brought them back
meaning: David led Israel's troops out to battle and brought them home safely; he was their real leader.
God will punish wrongdoing in David's heir with the kind of discipline humans receive, as a father corrects a son, to correct him and not to destroy him or take back his favor.

idiom: they would extinguish my one remaining ember
meaning: Killing her only surviving son would put out the last live coal of her household, wiping out her one remaining hope and her husband's name and family line.
An expression of utter contempt: the person is vile, worthless and despicable.

idiom: at the blast of the breath of His nostrils
meaning: A picture of God's angry snorting, His furious rebuke, felt as a storm wind strong enough to drive back the sea and lay bare the earth's foundations, as at the Red Sea.

idiom: the blood of the men who risked their lives
meaning: Putting their lives in serious danger to do something. David saw the water as costing their lives, so drinking it would be like drinking their blood.

idiom: go the way of all the earth
meaning: To be about to die, taking the road every human must take sooner or later.
To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: at the expense of his life
meaning: Adonijah's request would cost him his life; by making it he had brought his own death on himself.
To turn the heart toward the LORD fully and willingly, loving, fearing, and serving him alone. This means giving up any hidden attachment to other gods, including idols of the heart.
Passersby will make a hissing sound in scorn and mockery at the ruined temple, showing contempt for the fallen people.

idiom: I will scourge you with scorpions
meaning: The new king threatens to rule far more harshly than his father. Whips stand for a lighter punishment, and "scorpions" for something much more painful, probably a lash fitted with barbs or metal points, or simply a figure of speech for cruel treatment.
A rallying cry to break away: renounce loyalty to David's royal house and go home to look after themselves, leaving David's line to rule only its own tribe.

idiom: as one burns up dung until it is gone
meaning: God will wipe out Jeroboam's family completely and with contempt, clearing away every last trace of it the way people get rid of filthy refuse they find disgusting.
Whom I serve. It names the speaker as God's servant and minister, standing ready to do His will and speaking with His authority.
Kept on the queen's payroll: the prophets were fed and supported out of Jezebel's royal household supplies, a sign of her special favor and her backing of their cult.

idiom: The one putting on his armor should not boast like one taking it off
meaning: A proverb: don't brag about winning before the fight is over. Only the man taking off his armor after the battle has earned the right to boast.

idiom: the chariots and horsemen of Israel
meaning: The prophet (Elijah) was Israel's real defense and strength. Through his counsel, prayers and standing with God he protected the nation better than its war chariots and cavalry, which were the chief military power of the time.

idiom: He used to pour water on the hands of Elijah
meaning: He was Elijah's personal servant and constant companion; pouring water for a master to wash his hands was a servant's job.

idiom: even if the LORD were to make windows in heaven
meaning: A mocking expression of disbelief. Even if God opened floodgates in the sky, as at the Flood, and rained down grain, such sudden plenty still could not happen.

idiom: Tuck your cloak under your belt
meaning: Gather up your long loose robe at the waist so you can move quickly; get ready to go in haste.

idiom: children have come to the point of birth, but there is no strength to deliver them
meaning: A saying for a desperate crisis: things have reached the deciding moment, but every human resource is gone and there is no strength left to get through it, like a woman in labor too weak to deliver.
To incline the ear is to bend it toward someone and listen closely. It asks for, or trusts in, God's attentive hearing and answering of prayer, even the quiet sighs of the oppressed.

idiom: grass on the rooftops, scorched before it is grown
meaning: Grass that sprouted in the thin soil of flat roofs soon dried up in the sun without ever ripening. It means something short-lived and useless, like enemies who perish before their plans come to anything.
To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.
Reuben had sex with his father Jacob's concubine Bilhah. This shameful sin against his father cost him the rights of the firstborn.

idiom: How can I drink the blood of these men who risked their lives?
meaning: Putting their lives in serious danger to do something. David saw the water as costing their lives, so drinking it would be like drinking their blood.

idiom: a spear like a weaver's beam
meaning: A detail that likens this giant's weapon to Goliath's, so that Benaiah's fight with him recalls David's combat with Goliath.
Adding "of God" was a Hebrew way of saying something is very great; it means a huge, mighty army.

A lasting agreement that cannot be broken. Salt keeps things from spoiling, it went with sacrifices, and sharing salt at a meal sealed friendship and loyalty, so a salt covenant stood for something permanent and binding.

To worship other gods or idols. Israel was seen as bound to God like a wife to a husband, so idolatry was treated as unfaithfulness in marriage. The phrase also fits the sexually impure rites that went with some pagan worship.
Merely human strength, which is weak and frail, in contrast to God's power; an "arm" means a helper or source of strength.
To encourage, support and enable people in their work; here the king's goodwill let them carry on and finish rebuilding the temple.
The people of Israel, set apart and consecrated to God by his covenant, a people meant to stay separate from other nations.

A common saying of that time: a person will give up anything to save himself. Satan uses it to claim that Job accepted his losses only because he himself was unharmed, and that he will turn on God once his own body is struck. Commentators disagree on how the saying worked literally, but agree on this point.
Boxed in by God on every side, like a traveler whose road is blocked or a prisoner, with no way out of his suffering and confusion. It reverses the earlier sense of God's protective hedge around Job.
Human bodies, which are made from dust and rest on it. They are weak, short-lived and easily destroyed.
To encourage, support and enable people in their work; here the king's goodwill let them carry on and finish rebuilding the temple.

idiom: lift up your hands to Him
meaning: Raising or spreading out the hands was the posture of prayer; it means to pray and ask God for help.

idiom: you are the people with whom wisdom itself will die
meaning: Sarcasm: Job mocks his friends for acting as though they alone hold all the wisdom in the world, so that it will vanish when they die.

idiom: fill his belly with the hot east wind
meaning: To fill your mind with empty, worthless ideas and then blow them out as loud, violent talk that does no good, like the hot, destructive desert wind.

idiom: He gnashes His teeth at me
meaning: Grinding the teeth is a sign of fierce anger and hostility, like a wild beast about to tear its prey. In Job 16:9 it pictures the attacker raging against the sufferer.

idiom: They have turned night into day
meaning: Most read it as Job's complaint about his friends: they pretended his dark time of suffering was really day and promised that good times were about to dawn. Others take it as Job's own sleepless misery, where night gives him no more rest than day does.
The entrance to the underworld, the realm of the dead, thought of as a locked prison under the earth that no one leaves; going down there means dying, so Job's hope would die and be buried with him.
The worst and deadliest disease that death produces, probably a wasting illness like Job's. As a firstborn was the strongest child, this is death's strongest offspring.
Death, pictured as a fearsome ruler that the wicked are finally marched off to.

idiom: injustice is broken like a tree
meaning: "Injustice" here stands for the unjust person. Like a tree that is broken and never grows again, the wicked person comes to an end and is forgotten. The sources differ on whether this is sudden or a quiet decay.

idiom: It claps its hands at him and hisses him out of his place
meaning: Clapping and hissing were public gestures of scorn and contempt; people mock the wicked man and are glad to see him fall and be driven away.
God turns away and withholds his favor and help, in anger or seeming indifference. He acts as if he takes no notice of his people's suffering and does not step in to rescue them.
The power of the wicked, already raised to commit violence or oppression, is crushed and made useless.

idiom: tilt the water jars of the heavens
meaning: The rain-filled clouds are pictured as water skins that only God can control. Most read it as God tipping them to pour rain on the earth; some read it as God holding the rain back.

A kiss was the customary way to pay homage and pledge loyalty to a king, so it means submitting to and honoring the king God has installed. Several sources reject the rendering "Son" and read it as pure homage to God, or as accepting instruction.

idiom: Shine the light of Your face upon us
meaning: A request for God's favor and kindness, a prayer that He would look on the speaker with grace and show His presence; it echoes the priestly blessing of Numbers 6.

The commentaries cover only the Ezekiel wording. There, God will bring his people, who are "dead" as a nation in exile, back to life and home to their land, as if raising them from their graves. The lands of exile are pictured as their graves. The sources do not explain "their throats are open graves."
Let their own schemes fail and turn back on them, so that their plots bring about their own downfall.
Like a woman in labor, the wicked man plans and strains to bring his harmful schemes to birth, but what he produces is falsehood and failure that comes back on himself.
A plea for God to take action and use His power, both to rescue the oppressed and to strike their oppressors.
To incline the ear is to bend it toward someone and listen closely. It asks for, or trusts in, God's attentive hearing and answering of prayer, even the quiet sighs of the oppressed.

Literally "a heart and a heart": speaking from one heart while hiding another, so saying one thing and meaning something else. It stands for deceit and insincerity, and sometimes for changing one's mind from day to day.
The wicked prey on God's people, robbing and ruining them as casually, greedily and routinely as they eat their daily meals, with no remorse; in effect they live off oppressing them.
To incline the ear is to bend it toward someone and listen closely. It asks for, or trusts in, God's attentive hearing and answering of prayer, even the quiet sighs of the oppressed.
The pupil of the eye, the most delicate and closely guarded part of the body; it stands for someone kept with the greatest care and tenderness, a deeply cherished object.
A gesture of mocking scorn toward someone in trouble, sometimes with a show of pretended horror or surprise at their fate.

To be heading for the grave. Most apply it to the poor and suffering who are close to dying, set against the rich; some widen it to all mortal people, and some report a reading that means those already dead.

idiom: lift up his soul to an idol
meaning: To set one's heart, desire, or devotion on something false or worthless, especially false gods, instead of being loyal to the true God.

idiom: Lift up your heads, O gates
meaning: Here it means Pharaoh called the two prisoners out and took up their cases to decide their fate. It works as a wordplay: one was raised back to his post, the other raised up to be hanged.
Completely forgotten, the way a dead man soon fades from people's memory and is no longer thought of.
In a moment of panic the psalmist felt that God had abandoned him, that he was beyond God's notice and protection and as good as lost.
Give one another a knowing wink, a sly signal of shared spite and gloating over the victim's downfall.
In this verse, to be destroyed or wiped out, as all living things were killed by the flood.
Grinding the teeth is a sign of fierce anger and hostility, like a wild beast about to tear its prey. In Job 16:9 it pictures the attacker raging against the sufferer.

God has given the speaker ears ready to hear and obey His will; what God wants is attentive obedience rather than ritual sacrifice. Some read it as an allusion to piercing a slave's ear to mark lifelong service, which leads to the same idea of devoted obedience.
One trouble follows right after another, like waves or roaring torrents calling to each other, until the person is completely overwhelmed by a flood of afflictions.
To become a proverb that others point to: a people held up by the nations as a familiar example of calamity and of being forsaken by its God, and mocked in jeering sayings and songs.
The king's mouth and speech are full of charm, kindness and persuasive power, a gift poured on him from above that shows God's favor rests on him.

Oil used to anoint people at feasts, weddings and other happy times, as opposed to mourning, when people did not anoint themselves. Being anointed with it means being given great joy and honor as a sign of God's favor. Christian commentators often apply it to the Messiah's exaltation or to the Spirit.
To die and rot in the grave. To "not see decay" means to escape death and the grave.

idiom: They devour my people like bread
meaning: The oppressors destroy God's people as naturally and readily as they eat their ordinary food, without any thought of God.
To be cut off by a sudden, violent death in the middle of life, as if the earth opened and swallowed them alive like Korah's rebels. Sheol is the grave or realm of the dead, not the place of torment.
He means to get up before daybreak to praise God, as if his songs would wake the dawn instead of the dawn waking him. It is a poetic way of showing eager devotion.
An expression of contempt and conquest: Moab is reduced to the lowliest household vessel, a basin for washing the feet, meaning it will be a subject people doing menial service.

idiom: upon Edom I toss My sandal
meaning: Edom will be conquered and humbled. Most sources picture it as the lowest slave, to whom a master throws his sandals to carry or clean. Others see a gesture of taking possession of land, or of trampling on a defeated enemy.
Becoming a joke among drinkers and party-goers, who made up mocking songs about the speaker. It means being publicly ridiculed and the gossip of the town.

idiom: May their table become a snare
meaning: A wish that the very comforts and good things of the enemies, their feasting and their sense of safety, would turn into the means of their sudden ruin, catching them like a baited trap.
Comes from the Eastern custom of lying face-down on the ground before a ruler; it means complete, humbled submission.
They show off their arrogance openly, wearing it like jewelry. The image is of a proud, stiff neck and a haughty bearing that everyone can see.
To talk proudly, arrogantly, and defiantly, with the head held high in insolence.
The manna: food sent down from heaven, where angels live, and so fine it seemed fit for angels. The Hebrew literally says "bread of the mighty," which some take to mean food rich enough for princes.

Unreliable, letting you down just when you need them. A faulty bow sends the arrow off course, drops it, or breaks, so the archer misses his target. Israel kept breaking its promises to God the same way.

idiom: cause Your face to shine upon us
meaning: A request for God's favor and kindness, a prayer that He would look on the speaker with grace and show His presence; it echoes the priestly blessing of Numbers 6.

Righteousness and peace come together in full harmony, like friends embracing after being apart. It mainly describes qualities of God working together to save His people, and the people may reflect the same qualities.
To turn one's whole heart, desire and prayer toward God with sincere, eager devotion.
The horn, as on a strong wild ox, stands for strength and power. Raising someone's horn means giving them strength, victory and honor over their enemies.

To weigh honestly how short and uncertain life is, so as to live wisely in light of it. Ellicott instead takes God as the one allotting the days, and reads it as a prayer that he make people know the power of his anger as he does so.
The grave or the world of the dead, a place of stillness. Saying he would have dwelt there means he came close to dying.

To worship other gods or idols. Israel was seen as bound to God like a wife to a husband, so idolatry was treated as unfaithfulness in marriage. The phrase also fits the sexually impure rites that went with some pagan worship.

The sources disagree. Most say it means the king's young warriors coming to him eagerly, as fresh, sparkling and countless as morning dew. Others say it means the king's own youthful strength, always renewed. Some take it as a huge number of followers or offspring.

idiom: his horn will be lifted high in honor
meaning: The horn, as on a strong wild ox, stands for strength and power. Raising someone's horn means giving them strength, victory and honor over their enemies.

idiom: like a wineskin dried up by smoke
meaning: A leather wine bottle hung in a smoky house turns black, dry and shriveled. It pictures someone worn down and disfigured by suffering and grief.

idiom: the shade on your right hand
meaning: To have someone at your right hand means having them close beside you as a protector, defender, or champion, like a fellow warrior standing on your right. It can also mark a place of honor.

idiom: whose quiver is full of them
meaning: Blessed with many sons. Sons are pictured as a warrior's arrows, so a full quiver means a large family of sons who give their father strength and protection against opponents.

idiom: The plowmen plowed over my back
meaning: A picture of cruel, drawn-out oppression of Israel, as if enemies had run a plow over its back. It recalls a lash cutting furrows into a slave's back. The long furrows mean the suffering was thorough and went on a long time.

Grass that sprouted in the thin soil of flat roofs soon dried up in the sun without ever ripening. It means something short-lived and useless, like enemies who perish before their plans come to anything.

idiom: may my right hand cease to function
meaning: A solemn self-curse: if the speaker forgot Jerusalem (for example by playing joyful music in exile), may his right hand lose its skill, especially for playing the harp, or become useless altogether.

The edge of the grave: being right at the point of death, as if about to be swallowed by the world of the dead. In the psalm, scattered bones lying at Sheol's opening show people crushed, helpless and close to death.
The right hand was raised when swearing an oath, so a lying right hand means people whose solemn oaths and pledges cannot be trusted.

idiom: incline your ear to my sayings
meaning: To bend down and listen carefully to the teacher's words because they matter greatly.
The final outcome is extremely bitter and harmful. Wormwood was seen as both bitter and poisonous, so the pleasure at first ends in misery and ruin.
The "fountain" stands for a man's own wife; the wish is that she be blessed, mainly with children, and that he find his joy in her rather than in other women.
Making secret signals with the feet, such as shuffling, scraping, or pressing another's foot, to pass hidden messages to partners in a deceitful scheme.
A sly wink betrays secret malice, scheming with accomplices, or mockery, and it brings trouble on others.
Will end up with nothing. The man who harms his own household, whether by greed, harshness or bad management, gains nothing solid in the end, and what he has slips away.
What a person says produces results. Good, wise and kind speech brings good things back to the speaker himself.
Most take it as the bright, joyful look in someone's eyes, which cheers whoever sees it; others take it as the light or pleasant sights the eyes take in.
Pressing or biting the lips is a facial sign of a sly, malicious person who has already settled on harm; some see it as a signal to partners in crime.
A sly wink betrays secret malice, scheming with accomplices, or mockery, and it brings trouble on others.
To shake hands to seal a deal in which you promise to pay another person's debt if they fail; the proverb calls this rash.
To take in wrongdoing greedily and with pleasure, like a tasty morsel. The wicked enjoy doing evil and feed on it.

idiom: The spirit of a man is the lamp of the LORD
meaning: The God-given human spirit, the breath of life from God that gives self-awareness and conscience, works like a lamp God has lit inside a person. It shines into the hidden depths of the heart and judges the person's thoughts and motives.

idiom: The king's heart is a waterway in the hand of the LORD
meaning: Just as a farmer steers irrigation water into whatever channel he wants, God steers even a king's will and decisions to serve His purposes.

idiom: A wicked man hardens his face
meaning: To put on a bold, shameless face: stubborn defiance that ignores rebuke, does not blush at sin and will not admit fault.

idiom: put a knife to your throat
meaning: Hold back your appetite with the strictest self-control when you eat at a ruler's table, as if a blade were at your throat. Some read it as a warning instead: overindulging there could cost you your life.

idiom: heap burning coals on his head
meaning: Being kind to an enemy makes him burn with shame and regret, which may move him to repent. Others take it as the most effective kind of revenge, or as adding to God's judgment on him.

Speech that glows with warm claims of love and friendship while hiding a wicked heart, a fine surface over something worthless. One source prefers a different reading: lips burning with malice and slander.

idiom: The wounds of a friend are faithful
meaning: A true friend's honest criticism may hurt, but it comes from real love and does you good. It is better than an enemy's many kisses, which are empty or false.
He deliberately looks away from the poor, or pretends not to see them, so he will not have to feel pity or help.
God gives the light of life to both poor and oppressor; both owe their existence to Him and depend on Him as maker and judge.

idiom: She eats and wipes her mouth
meaning: The adulteress commits her sin in secret, removes every trace of it the way someone wipes away signs of a meal, and then claims she is innocent. "Eating" is a polite way of referring to the sexual act.
She prepares for her work with energy and determination, as people tucked up their long robes with a belt before hard work; strength is pictured as the belt she puts on.
On earth, in this present world of human life and work. The phrase is used this way only in Ecclesiastes, and some sources compare it to similar Greek expressions and to the English word "sublunary."
The pose of a lazy person who keeps his hands idle instead of working, which leads to his own ruin and poverty.
He spends his whole life in gloom and misery, with no joy or light in his days.
Living people, those who are alive under the sun.

In this verse, going in and out of the holy place most likely means regularly frequenting the place of worship or seat of judgment, carrying on one's public life; the verse is read in many different ways.

idiom: Cast your bread upon the waters
meaning: Give freely and generously to others, especially the poor, even when it looks wasted and you can't expect anything back. In time the good you did will come back to you.
To join with others in a deal or pact; here Israel was making agreements and alliances (trade, marriage, or political) with foreign peoples and taking up their ways, which God's law forbade.
God's anger is not satisfied yet and his punishment is not over. The blows already struck are only the start, and more judgment is still to come.

The two hostile kings (Rezin of Aram and Pekah) are like the burnt-out ends of torches: they give off smoke but no real fire. They are nearly spent, they look more dangerous than they are, and they will soon go out, so there is no reason to fear them.
God turns away and withholds his favor and help, in anger or seeming indifference. He acts as if he takes no notice of his people's suffering and does not step in to rescue them.

The Lord overthrows his enemy with nothing more than what comes from his mouth (his breath or word), which shows his overwhelming power and how little effort it costs him. Some take it as the spoken gospel working over time, others as his power at his return, but either way his word alone is enough.
The King's spoken word, acting like a ruler's scepter or a rod of punishment. His verdicts are so just and powerful that they strike down the wicked and oppressors with no other weapon needed.
Hands hanging down helplessly: an image of terror and despair, losing all courage and strength to act or fight back.
People lost all courage and hope from fear, as if their hearts had turned to water, leaving them no strength to act or resist.
God's power is already at work to carry out what He has planned, and nobody can stop it or turn it aside.

idiom: head or tail, palm or reed
meaning: Everyone in Egypt, from the highest rank to the lowest, is helpless; no one can do anything that works.

idiom: the key to the house of David
meaning: The badge of the top steward's office over the royal palace, meaning full authority over the king's household and affairs; he alone decided who got access.
A boast of false safety: people acting as if they had a deal with death and the grave that kept them from harm, while really trusting lies (likely a secret political alliance) rather than God.

idiom: You conceive chaff; you give birth to stubble
meaning: The enemy's plans and efforts will come to nothing, worthless like chaff and stubble, and their own rage will be what destroys them.

idiom: your neck is iron and your forehead is bronze
meaning: You are utterly stubborn, refusing God's yoke like an ox stiffening its neck, and shameless, never blushing at your sin.

idiom: Is My hand too short to redeem you
meaning: A shortened hand was a picture of weakness, and a long outstretched hand a picture of power. God asks whether his power has shrunk. It has not: he can still rescue his people as he did at the Exodus, so their troubles do not come from his weakness.

To suffer the share of God's anger and punishment that is assigned to someone, pictured as a cup they are made to drink. In Jeremiah 49:12 the point is that if even God's own people were made to suffer it, Edom has no hope of escaping.
God gets ready to act with force, like a warrior pulling back his sleeve or cloak to free his arm for battle. He steps in openly and powerfully for His people, where all nations can see it.
Like sheep with no shepherd, everyone has wandered away from God, each following his own selfish path toward danger and ruin.

idiom: ride on the heights of the land
meaning: To live in triumph, safety, and command, like a conqueror holding the high ground and strongholds of a country. In other words, to have full and secure possession of the land and a place of honor.
To be fed and enriched by the wealth and support of foreign nations and their kings, given freely to God's people the way a mother nurses a baby.
The leaders threw off God's law and refused to obey, like oxen that break loose from the yoke and its straps and wander off.
Hands hanging down helplessly: an image of terror and despair, losing all courage and strength to act or fight back.
To listen with real attention; here the people would not give God even a partial hearing.
To bend the ear toward someone and really listen; the people refused to listen to and heed God's commands.

idiom: the ears of all who hear of it will ring
meaning: The news will be so shocking and terrible that anyone who hears it will be stunned, as if both ears had been struck.
Prophets who speak only from themselves, with no message from God, yet use the solemn formula "the LORD declares" so their own words pass as divine oracles.
Struck by God's judgment through the sword, the nations reel and act wildly, like drunk men who have lost their reason from terror.
Hands hanging down helplessly: an image of terror and despair, losing all courage and strength to act or fight back.

To suffer the share of God's anger and punishment that is assigned to someone, pictured as a cup they are made to drink. In Jeremiah 49:12 the point is that if even God's own people were made to suffer it, Edom has no hope of escaping.

idiom: without a hand turned to help her
meaning: Sodom was destroyed in a moment by God alone, with no human hands at work against it. Jerusalem, by contrast, suffered long and cruelly at the hands of human enemies.
The king, as the Lord's anointed, was the center of the nation's life. The people's survival and hopes as a nation depended on him, as much as life depends on breath.
Hearts unfaithful to God that turned to idols. Worshiping idols is pictured as being unfaithful in a marriage (spiritual adultery).

idiom: every knee will turn to water
meaning: Total loss of strength and nerve from terror: legs trembling and giving way, with no power left to resist. Some note it may also refer to the sweat or loss of bladder control that fear causes.

idiom: putting the branch to their nose
meaning: Probably a gesture from idol worship, perhaps holding a twig or bundle of branches up to the face while praying to the sun, as Persian sun-worshippers did. The custom is now unclear. Others take it as a gesture of scorn or an insult aimed at God.

idiom: The city is the cooking pot, and we are the meat
meaning: Jerusalem's leaders mocked the prophets' warnings: the city's walls would shield them from the enemy the way a pot keeps meat from the fire, so they were safe and judgment was not near. One commentator instead reads it as a grim saying of despair, that they were trapped and doomed to cook inside.
Raising the hand toward heaven was the gesture for taking an oath, so the phrase means God swore a solemn oath and bound himself to his promise.
People lost all courage and hope from fear, as if their hearts had turned to water, leaving them no strength to act or resist.
People lost all courage and hope from fear, as if their hearts had turned to water, leaving them no strength to act or resist.
To step into the broken spot in the wall and stand between the people and God's coming judgment, pleading for them or turning things around so the land is not destroyed, as Moses once did.

idiom: set your face against the Ammonites
meaning: The prophet was to look toward the Ammonites' land with a stern, threatening expression and boldly announce judgment on them.

idiom: The gate to the nations is broken
meaning: Jerusalem had been a gateway that the trade and traffic of many peoples passed through, and it stood between Tyre and that business. Now that it was destroyed, Tyre gloated that the commerce would come to her instead.
The prophet was to turn his gaze and his words toward Sidon with a stern look and announce its coming ruin.
The exiles' cry of despair: as a nation they are finished, severed like a limb or branch, with no hope of revival or return.
Put away the inner stubbornness, corrupt desires, and dullness toward God. Make real in the heart the purity and devotion to God that outward circumcision stood for.

idiom: the Messiah will be cut off
meaning: The anointed one would be violently removed from among the living, usually read as being put to death. Most of these sources say this is Jesus, while Cambridge thinks it is the high priest Onias III.

To worship other gods or idols. Israel was seen as bound to God like a wife to a husband, so idolatry was treated as unfaithfulness in marriage. The phrase also fits the sexually impure rites that went with some pagan worship.

idiom: they have played the harlot against their God
meaning: To worship other gods or idols. Israel was seen as bound to God like a wife to a husband, so idolatry was treated as unfaithfulness in marriage. The phrase also fits the sexually impure rites that went with some pagan worship.

idiom: The whirlwind has wrapped them in its wings
meaning: Israel will be carried off suddenly and with unstoppable force into exile in a distant land, as if swept up and away by a whirlwind.

Moving a neighbor's landmark was a cursed crime of taking what is not yours. The princes acted like such people, recklessly ignoring the limits of right set by God and the rights of others (some add literal land-grabbing or idolatry).

Through mixing with the pagan nations, Israel had become worthless, like a flat loaf left unturned on the coals: burnt on one side, raw on the other and fit for neither use. Most see an inconsistent people who claim to worship the LORD but follow pagan ways; Cambridge suggests a nation half-ruined by disasters.

idiom: Where, O Death, are your plagues? Where, O Sheol, is your sting?
meaning: Most sources read it as a triumphant taunt over a defeated enemy: death and the grave have lost their power to hurt God's people, whom He will rescue. Others read it as God calling on death and Sheol to bring out their plagues and strike rebellious Israel.

idiom: For three transgressions of Damascus, even four
meaning: Not an exact count. It is a stock Hebrew rising-number saying for many repeated sins, with the last one pushing the guilt past the limit, so God's judgment will not be called back.

idiom: For three transgressions of Israel, even four
meaning: Not an exact count. It is a stock Hebrew rising-number saying for many repeated sins, with the last one pushing the guilt past the limit, so God's judgment will not be called back.
Famine: teeth stay clean because there is no food to eat.

idiom: like a firebrand snatched from a blaze
meaning: A charred stick pulled out of the fire just in time; a narrow escape from complete destruction, though not without damage.
To twist justice, which should be sweet and healing, into something bitter and cruel for those who receive it, through corrupt judgment and oppression.
David's royal house and kingdom, brought down from a palace to something like a broken-down hut. God promises to rebuild it, a promise many link to the Messiah.

idiom: so all the nations will drink continually
meaning: To suffer the share of God's anger and punishment that is assigned to someone, pictured as a cup they are made to drink. In Jeremiah 49:12 the point is that if even God's own people were made to suffer it, Edom has no hope of escaping.
A vivid picture of being as good as dead, swallowed into the world of the dead with no apparent way out.

idiom: cannot tell their right hand from their left
meaning: Describes young children too young to tell even basic things apart, and so not yet able to judge right from wrong or be held morally responsible.
A poetic name for the people of Jerusalem (Zion), pictured as a woman.
A false prophet whose message is as empty and worthless as wind, who tells people the pleasant lies they want to hear, such as promises of plenty and good living.

idiom: walk in the name of their gods
meaning: To shape one's whole life and conduct around one's god, staying loyal to it and relying on its power and protection. The nations do this with their worthless gods, while Israel lives in steady loyalty to the LORD and draws its strength from Him.

idiom: let us feast our eyes on Zion
meaning: To gaze at Zion's ruin and humiliation with spiteful pleasure.

idiom: seven shepherds, even eight leaders of men
meaning: A full and more-than-enough number of capable leaders; seven stands for a complete number and adding eight means even more than needed, so God will raise up plenty of rulers to drive back the invader.

idiom: the stones will cry out from the wall
meaning: Even the building materials of a house or empire built with stolen wealth and forced labor will act as witnesses. They accuse the builder of his injustice and call down judgment on him.

idiom: they rose early to corrupt all their deeds
meaning: They did evil eagerly and on purpose, wasting no time and putting all their effort into it, like people who get up at dawn to start important work.

idiom: do not let your hands fall limp
meaning: Hands hanging down helplessly: an image of terror and despair, losing all courage and strength to act or fight back.

idiom: lifted up their horns against the land of Judah
meaning: A horn stood for strength and power. Lifting it means nations proudly using their power to attack and crush Judah.

idiom: sit under your own vine and fig tree
meaning: A picture of peaceful, safe, prosperous life, like the days of Solomon, with neighbors gathering and enjoying friendly company together.
A time of humble, unimpressive beginnings, like the modest start on rebuilding the temple. It should not be looked down on, because God watches over the work with favor and will see it finished.
To encourage, support and enable people in their work; here the king's goodwill let them carry on and finish rebuilding the temple.

idiom: this magnificent price at which they valued me
meaning: Bitter irony: the thirty silver pieces were an insultingly small wage (about the price of a slave), showing how little they valued the shepherd. It was fit only to be thrown to the potter.

idiom: living water will flow out from Jerusalem
meaning: In everyday speech it meant flowing spring water, not still water. Jesus used it for the life-giving grace and Spirit He gives, which truly satisfies the soul.

God did not choose Esau and his descendants, Edom, for the special favor He gave Jacob, and in that sense rejected him. This is relative rather than active hatred: Edom was left in ruin while Israel was restored.

idiom: His winnowing fork is in His hand
meaning: The coming Messiah is ready to sort the good from the bad, just as a farmer tosses threshed grain into the wind to separate wheat from chaff. He will gather the righteous safely and destroy the worthless, ending the present mixture of the two.

People who are humble inside and know they have nothing of their own to offer God. They feel their need, rely on his mercy and do not trust in themselves; they are the opposite of the spiritually proud. Luke's shorter form points to the literally poor, but Matthew's wording is not limited to them.

idiom: not a single jot, not a stroke of a pen
meaning: Not even the smallest detail of the Law, down to its tiniest letter or the smallest mark on a letter, will be lost until all it was meant to do has happened.

idiom: if your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away
meaning: Strict self-denial: give up even your most valued abilities or possessions, which a right hand stands for, if they draw you into sin, because losing them is better than being lost.

idiom: Eye for eye and tooth for tooth
meaning: The law that the penalty must match the injury, no more and no less. It was a rule for judges and courts, not a license for personal revenge, and was often settled by a matching payment rather than literal maiming.

The eye is the body's lamp. A good (sound, single) eye stands for an inner sight fixed steadily on one goal, God and heavenly treasure, and that lights up the whole life. Gill instead uses the Jewish idiom in which a good eye means a generous spirit and an evil eye a stingy one.

idiom: The eye is the lamp of the body
meaning: Just as the eye lets light in and guides the whole body, a person's inner outlook (mind, conscience or heart) guides their whole life. If that inner eye is clear and fixed on God alone, the whole life is filled with light. One source takes a good eye to mean a generous spirit, in line with Jewish usage.
Grinding the teeth is a sign of fierce anger and hostility, like a wild beast about to tear its prey. In Job 16:9 it pictures the attacker raging against the sufferer.

idiom: let the dead bury their own dead
meaning: A play on two meanings of "dead": let those who are spiritually dead, and have no interest in God's kingdom, handle burying the physically dead. Following Christ must come before even the most sacred family duty.

idiom: No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment
meaning: Joining something new to something old does not fit and only makes the damage worse. Some take it that Jesus' teaching is not a patch to mend the old religious system; others that strict duties such as fasting should not be imposed on disciples not yet ready for them.

idiom: We played the flute for you, and you did not dance
meaning: Taken from children in the marketplace who play at weddings and funerals and complain that their sulky friends join neither game. It describes people who cannot be pleased whatever is offered: they rejected John's strict, mournful way and also Jesus' joyful, ordinary way of living.

idiom: It is not right to take the children's bread and toss it to the dogs
meaning: A common saying of the time: the "children" were the Jews, God's people, and "dogs" was a scornful name for Gentiles. It meant the blessings meant first for Israel should not be handed to outsiders ahead of them. Jesus used it to test the woman's faith, not to approve the insult.

idiom: Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees
meaning: Watch out for the Pharisees' corrupting influence, which Luke names as hypocrisy, a show of holiness that isn't real. Like yeast, it works unseen and slowly spreads until it affects everything.

idiom: Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven
meaning: In Jewish usage, "binding" and "loosing" meant declaring something forbidden or allowed. The apostles are given authority to rule on what is required or permitted in the church, and to admit or exclude people, and heaven will confirm those decisions.

idiom: If your hand or your foot causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away
meaning: Firmly give up anything that leads you into sin, whether pursuits, possessions or friendships, however dear. Going to life without them is better than keeping them and being lost.

idiom: Can you drink the cup I am going to drink?
meaning: Jesus asks if they can endure the bitter suffering God has given him. In Scripture a cup is a person's appointed lot, often affliction or God's wrath.
To hold the recognized authority to teach and explain the Law of Moses, as his successors in that role; Jewish teachers sat down when they explained Scripture.

idiom: You strain out a gnat but swallow a camel
meaning: A proverb for being fussy over the tiniest points of the law while ignoring huge sins; strict Jews filtered drinks to avoid swallowing a tiny unclean insect, yet these leaders took in something as large and unclean as a camel.

idiom: Fill up, then, the measure of the sin of your fathers
meaning: Ironic permission that is really a prediction: go ahead and finish the evil your ancestors began, by killing Christ and his messengers, until the full limit of guilt is reached and God's punishment falls.

idiom: Wherever there is a carcass, there the vultures will gather
meaning: A proverb: just as vultures surely and quickly find a dead body, judgment will surely arrive wherever corruption is. Many apply it to the Roman armies descending on corrupt Jerusalem. Others apply it to God's agents of destruction in general, to everyone gathering before Christ for judgment, or to the certainty of recognizing His coming.

idiom: let this cup pass from Me
meaning: To suffer the share of God's anger and punishment that is assigned to someone, pictured as a cup they are made to drink. In Jeremiah 49:12 the point is that if even God's own people were made to suffer it, Edom has no hope of escaping.

idiom: if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it
meaning: The "cup" means the portion or lot God assigns to a person; here Jesus asks to be spared the suffering ahead of him, while yielding to the Father's will.

idiom: sitting at the right hand of Power
meaning: To have someone at your right hand means having them close beside you as a protector, defender, or champion, like a fellow warrior standing on your right. It can also mark a place of honor.

idiom: His blood be on us and on our children
meaning: The guilt and responsibility for a person's death rests on that person (or on whoever is named), not on anyone else. Someone who dies through his own neglect or choice has only himself to blame.
To have died. Sleep is the usual gentle picture for death, especially a believer's death.

idiom: He is out of His mind
meaning: His family thought He had lost control of Himself, carried away by intense zeal and overwork; it was a disturbed state rather than outright insanity.

idiom: If your hand causes you to sin, cut it off
meaning: Not meant literally: give up anything that leads you into sin, even something as dear and useful as a hand, whether a habit, a pleasure or a close friend. Any loss is better than ending in hell.

idiom: everyone will be salted with fire
meaning: Many read it as fiery trial and self-denial that purify Christ's followers and make them acceptable to God, like salt on a sacrifice. Others read it as the wicked being kept from being consumed in unending punishment, the way salt preserves. Some apply it to both.
The "cup" means the portion or lot God assigns to a person; here Jesus asks to be spared the suffering ahead of him, while yielding to the Father's will.
The horn, as on a strong wild ox, stands for strength and power. Raising someone's horn means giving them strength, victory and honor over their enemies.
To be given a generous return, handed right to you. The "lap" is the large fold of a robe over the chest, which people used as a pocket. The measure is pictured as grain pressed down and overflowing.
To stumble over Jesus: to be put off by him, or by the way he came and acted, and so to doubt or reject him.
Shallow believers give up their faith and abandon the message when hardship or persecution tests them.

idiom: Your eye is the lamp of your body
meaning: Just as the eye lets light in and guides the whole body, a person's inner outlook (mind, conscience or heart) guides their whole life. If that inner eye is clear and fixed on God alone, the whole life is filled with light. One source takes a good eye to mean a generous spirit, in line with Jewish usage.
Watch out for the Pharisees' corrupting influence, which Luke names as hypocrisy, a show of holiness that isn't real. Like yeast, it works unseen and slowly spreads until it affects everything.

idiom: to ignite a fire on the earth
meaning: Sources differ on what the fire is: judgment that purifies and destroys, conflict and division (with suffering) caused by the gospel, or the new spiritual life and Spirit Jesus brings. Cambridge takes it in all these senses.
A contemptuous name for Herod, calling him a sly, cunning, scheming man who works by trickery; the fox stood for craftiness and sneaky attack.

idiom: your house is left to you desolate
meaning: Your house (the temple and city) is abandoned by God and left to you alone; his presence has gone and ruin will soon follow.
To accept willingly whatever suffering following Jesus brings, including denying oneself, shame, persecution, and even death.

The happy state of the righteous after death. At meals people reclined with their head near the chest of the person beside them, so lying next to Abraham meant being an honored guest close to him at the heavenly banquet.
To have someone at your right hand means having them close beside you as a protector, defender, or champion, like a fellow warrior standing on your right. It can also mark a place of honor.
Enemies fully defeated and put under the ruler's feet, under his complete control.
Take heart and look up with hopeful expectation instead of hanging the head in dejection, because deliverance is near.

idiom: sift all of you like wheat
meaning: Satan wants to shake and test the disciples hard with temptation and trouble, the way grain is tossed in a sieve, hoping to show their faith is worthless chaff.

idiom: seated at the right hand of the power of God
meaning: To have someone at your right hand means having them close beside you as a protector, defender, or champion, like a fellow warrior standing on your right. It can also mark a place of honor.

idiom: if men do these things while the tree is green, what will happen when it is dry?
meaning: This is a proverb arguing from lesser to greater. A green tree does not burn easily, but a dry one does. If such suffering falls on the innocent one, far worse will come on the guilty, which several sources link to the coming Roman judgment on the nation.

idiom: My hour has not yet come
meaning: The right moment for Jesus to act had not yet arrived. That moment was set by God, not by others, and in it he would show his power as Messiah. He signals that he will act, but at his own time.

idiom: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again
meaning: A riddle-like prediction. "Temple" means Jesus' own body: when they kill him, he will rise from the dead on the third day, and that will be the sign of his authority.

The groom's closest friend, who arranged the marriage and ran the wedding feast. He shared fully in the groom's happiness. John the Baptist used it of himself: he had prepared the people for the Messiah and was glad to step back once the people went to Him.
In everyday speech it meant flowing spring water, not still water. Jesus used it for the life-giving grace and Spirit He gives, which truly satisfies the soul.
God the Father authenticated and endorsed Jesus as the one He sent to give lasting life, the way a seal confirms a document; He did this through miracles, Scripture and the voice from heaven.

idiom: eat the flesh and drink the blood of the Son of Man
meaning: Not literal. It means taking Christ himself, and especially his sacrificial death, into your inner life through faith, as the one source of spiritual life. Mentioning blood separately from flesh points to his violent death, and the words would have shocked Jews, who were forbidden to eat blood.

idiom: His hour had not yet come
meaning: The time God had set for Jesus' suffering and death (his departure to the Father) had arrived. Before that moment his enemies could only plot against him and could not touch him.
Satan, as the ruler of the world that stands against God. Jewish teachers commonly used this title for Satan, whom they saw as lord of the Gentiles. Jesus says his death will overthrow him.

idiom: has lifted up his heel against Me
meaning: Like a horse that kicks the master who feeds it, or a wrestler who trips someone up. It means a trusted friend who shared his table turned on him in brutal betrayal.
A Hebrew way of describing someone by his defining trait: a man marked by ruin and headed for it. Here it means Judas, the one disciple who was lost.

idiom: He is at my right hand
meaning: To have someone at your right hand means having them close beside you as a protector, defender, or champion, like a fellow warrior standing on your right. It can also mark a place of honor.

idiom: to the right hand of God
meaning: To have someone at your right hand means having them close beside you as a protector, defender, or champion, like a fellow warrior standing on your right. It can also mark a place of honor.
People far from God's people: mainly the Gentiles, and possibly also Jews scattered in other lands or later generations.

idiom: completely cut off from among his people
meaning: In this verse, to be destroyed or wiped out, as all living things were killed by the flood.
Putting Jesus to death by crucifixion; "tree" stands for the cross.

idiom: You stiff-necked people with uncircumcised hearts and ears
meaning: Stubborn and rebellious. The picture is a work animal that stiffens its neck and refuses to be steered by its driver or to accept the yoke.

idiom: at the right hand of God
meaning: To have someone at your right hand means having them close beside you as a protector, defender, or champion, like a fellow warrior standing on your right. It can also mark a place of honor.

idiom: You are out of your mind
meaning: "You're crazy!": a reaction to news that seemed too good to be true, since they thought what she said was impossible.

idiom: a man after My own heart
meaning: A man God chose who fits what God wants, someone who would carry out God's will (David, in contrast to Saul).
To die and rot in the grave. To "not see decay" means to escape death and the grave.
To die and rot in the grave. To "not see decay" means to escape death and the grave.
To die and rot in the grave. To "not see decay" means to escape death and the grave.
They exposed themselves to deadly danger, as in the persecution and stoning on their journeys, for the cause of Christ.

idiom: Your blood be on your own heads!
meaning: The guilt and responsibility for a person's death rests on that person (or on whoever is named), not on anyone else. Someone who dies through his own neglect or choice has only himself to blame.
To share the Lord's Supper (communion), held by early Christians when they met on the first day of the week, possibly together with a shared meal.
You hypocrite: like a wall coated with whitewash, you look fair and righteous on the outside but are not what you seem underneath.

idiom: It is hard for you to kick against the goads
meaning: Taken from an ox that kicks back at the driver's pointed stick and only hurts itself more; resisting God, who is far stronger, is useless and self-harming, so it is better to give in.
As far as his human nature and human ancestry go, in contrast to his divine nature as Son of God.
To live and direct one's conduct by the rule and impulses of fallen, sin-dominated human nature, instead of being led by God's Spirit; "walking" stands for the whole direction of one's life.

idiom: put to death the deeds of the body
meaning: To kill off sinful desires and habits completely. That means refusing to feed or tolerate them, so that they lose all their power.

idiom: How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news
meaning: Messengers who bring news of deliverance and salvation are a welcome, delightful sight, like a runner seen coming over the hills with good news. They are loved because of the message they carry.
Saved only narrowly and with difficulty, losing the work he built, like someone who barely escapes a fire while everything he had is burned up.

idiom: Get rid of the old leaven
meaning: Remove the old sin and corruption, including the offender and the attitude that put up with him, from the church, as Jews searched out every crumb of leaven before Passover. That way the community would really be as pure as its calling says.

idiom: drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons
meaning: Drinking at the Lord's Supper means fellowship with Christ, and drinking the wine offered at idol feasts means fellowship with the demons behind the idols. A believer cannot rightly share in both.
To have died. Sleep is the usual gentle picture for death, especially a believer's death.
Outsiders hearing nothing but uninterpreted tongues would think the congregation were raving fanatics or insane.
To have died. Sleep is the usual gentle picture for death, especially a believer's death.
To have died. Sleep is the usual gentle picture for death, especially a believer's death.

Most take it as a figure: Paul faced deadly danger at Ephesus from savage, beast-like opponents, since a Roman citizen could not legally be thrown to animals. Gill argues for a literal fight in the arena, or a supposed case.
To have died. Sleep is the usual gentle picture for death, especially a believer's death.

Being unreliable: saying yes and no about the same thing, changing plans on a whim like worldly people do. Some take it the other way, as stubbornly forcing one's yes to stay yes no matter what, and one source calls the clause's exact sense uncertain.

God has marked believers as His own and confirmed that they are genuine. A seal stamped on a document or property showed ownership, made it official, and kept it secure. God's seal is the gift of His Spirit, which assures believers that they belong to Him.
Unlike Moses, who veiled his face, and unlike those with a veil over their hearts, believers see the Lord's glory openly and clearly, with nothing in between.

idiom: the earthly tent we live in
meaning: The mortal body is a temporary dwelling for the soul, like a tent that is easily taken down. At death it is dismantled, and God provides a permanent home.
Critics called Paul mad for his intense zeal, ecstasies and bold claims; he answers that whatever looks like madness is done for God.

Being bound in a close partnership with unbelievers, as mismatched as an ox and a donkey hitched to the same plow, which the Mosaic law forbade. It includes marriage but also extends to other intimate ties, such as joining in idol worship, because believers and unbelievers have no common ground.
Paul admits that boasting about himself is like talking as a madman, perhaps throwing his critics' insult back at them, but he is forced into it to answer his rivals.

Clasping right hands was a sign of friendship and agreement; by it the Jerusalem leaders publicly recognized Paul and Barnabas as true partners and colleagues in the work, sealing a pledge to the same gospel with separate mission fields.

idiom: you have fallen away from grace
meaning: Anyone who tries to be made right with God by keeping the law gives up the way of God's free favor through Christ, and so loses their place in it.

idiom: seated Him at His right hand
meaning: To have someone at your right hand means having them close beside you as a protector, defender, or champion, like a fellow warrior standing on your right. It can also mark a place of honor.
To make the most of every opportunity. Like a merchant buying up a valuable item, you seize each chance to do good and use it well, because an evil age is full of distractions and temptations.

idiom: poured out like a drink offering
meaning: Giving up one's life, here Paul's possible death as a martyr, as an offering to God. It alludes to the wine poured over or beside a sacrifice. Paul pictures his blood as that libation, added to the sacrifice of his converts' faith.

"Dog" was an insult for someone unclean, shameless, snarling, and outcast. Jews used it for Gentiles. Paul turns it back on the Judaizing teachers, saying they are the true outsiders and troublemakers.

idiom: seated at the right hand of God
meaning: To have someone at your right hand means having them close beside you as a protector, defender, or champion, like a fellow warrior standing on your right. It can also mark a place of honor.
To kill off sinful desires and habits completely. That means refusing to feed or tolerate them, so that they lose all their power.
Speech that is wholesome, pleasant, and to the point. Salt both preserves food and gives it flavor, so this speech is neither corrupt nor dull, and it fits each person who asks a question.

idiom: those who have fallen asleep in Him
meaning: To have died. Sleep is the usual gentle picture for death, especially a believer's death.
To be removed or withdrawn. Once the restraining power is gone, the lawlessness that now works in secret will appear openly. Who the restrainer is remains disputed, but not what the phrase means.

The Lord overthrows his enemy with nothing more than what comes from his mouth (his breath or word), which shows his overwhelming power and how little effort it costs him. Some take it as the spoken gospel working over time, others as his power at his return, but either way his word alone is enough.

idiom: in season and out of season
meaning: It means at all times. The preacher should keep at the work urgently and seize every chance, whether the time suits him and his hearers or not, and even in danger or discouragement.

Hungry to hear something pleasing or new. Like an itch that wants scratching, these listeners crave teaching that flatters them and leaves their desires alone, and they collect teachers who will give them that.

idiom: being poured out like a drink offering
meaning: Giving up one's life, here Paul's possible death as a martyr, as an offering to God. It alludes to the wine poured over or beside a sacrifice. Paul pictures his blood as that libation, added to the sacrifice of his converts' faith.

idiom: refreshed the hearts of the saints
meaning: Philemon's love and generous help gave believers' inner feelings rest and relief from their troubles and burdens, cheering them deeply.

idiom: in the loin of his ancestor
meaning: Levi was not yet born, but he was counted as already present in his forefather Abraham. So what Abraham did, paying tithes to Melchizedek, was treated as done by his descendants too.
Enemies fully defeated and put under the ruler's feet, under his complete control.

A huge crowd (in Greek, Latin and Hebrew a "cloud" meant a great number) of earlier faithful people. They prove that faith pays off, and they are pictured all around believers like spectators in the stands at a race, which should push believers to keep going.
Spoken praise and thanksgiving to God, which the lips "bear" like fruit, offered as a sacrifice in place of the old animal and thank offerings.
Spiritually unfaithful people. Drawing on the Old Testament picture of God as husband to his people, those who love the world have broken faith with God, like a wife cheating on her husband.

idiom: You have fattened your hearts in the day of slaughter
meaning: The rich have indulged themselves to the full like cattle fattened for slaughter, feeding happily even as their day of judgment and ruin arrives. Some read it as living every day like a lavish feast after a sacrifice.

idiom: cover over a multitude of sins
meaning: To bring about the forgiveness of many sins, so they are hidden from God's judgment. Here it mainly means the sins of the person brought back from wrongdoing.
Before conversion people were like a flock with no shepherd: they had wandered off on their own paths, had no protector, and were in danger until they were brought back to the true Shepherd.

idiom: love covers over a multitude of sins
meaning: Love overlooks, forgives and does not expose the many faults of others, so it keeps the peace instead of stirring up strife.
The ruin decreed for them is not idle or put off. It is awake, watching them, and moving toward them, and it will strike at the appointed time, even if it seems to be delayed.
To help travelers on their journey by giving them supplies, hospitality, and sometimes an escort, and seeing them off with honor.
They followed Cain's way of life, the first great example of wickedness, marked by envy, hatred of the righteous and defiance of God.

Completely and hopelessly dead, like a barren tree pulled out by its roots that can never bear fruit again. Some sources read the "twice" as two deaths: dead in their natural state, then dead again after falling away from the faith they once professed.

False teachers who are unstable and unreliable, like heavenly bodies that do not keep a steady course. Sources compare them to planets that seem to wander, or to comets and meteors that blaze briefly and then vanish into darkness. Their fame is short and their influence harmful.

idiom: wild waves of the sea, foaming up their own shame
meaning: The false teachers are as restless, loud and uncontrolled as stormy waves, and like waves throwing up foam and filth, all their noise only shows off their own disgraceful deeds and empty teaching.
They kept themselves morally pure and true to their faith, not stained by the corruption around them.

Christ has full royal authority over God's house and kingdom, like the palace steward given the king's key in Isaiah 22:22. He alone decides who gets in and who is shut out, and no one can overrule him.
Being lukewarm: claiming faith but having no real zeal, neither burning with devotion nor openly untouched by it, a careless and self-satisfied state that Christ finds worse than either extreme.
The Messiah as the shoot that grows from David's family line: David's true descendant and heir, with the right to rule on his throne. Some add that he is also David's source and Lord.
A common sign of grief, mourning and humiliation, showing they had been brought low or shared another's sorrow.
To be cleansed from sin through the blood of Christ, the Lamb. This is what gives people the right to eat from the tree of life and enter the heavenly city.
